mean: to the great satisfaction of all (when wrongdoers are punished)

use.how: Used as a predicate or before 的 about news that a wrongdoer has been punished or a public wrong set right: 这个判决大快人心。

near.diff: 拍手称快 describes people clapping and cheering; 大快人心 describes the event itself as satisfying to the public.

cue: A gang that cheated hundreds of elderly people out of their savings is finally sentenced, and the whole town feels justice has been done.

ctx.s: 骗子终于被抓了，真是{大快人心}！
ctx.en: The swindler has finally been caught. Everyone is so glad!

ctx.s: 这家黑心工厂被查封的消息，可以说{大快人心}。
ctx.en: The news that the unscrupulous factory has been shut down has delighted everyone.

ctx.s: 法院对酒驾撞人者的重判，是一个{大快人心}的判决。
ctx.en: The heavy sentence for the drunk driver who hit a pedestrian is a verdict that satisfies the public.

ctx.s: “听说那个欺负同学的家伙被开除了？”“对，{大快人心}啊。”
ctx.en: "I heard the guy who bullied his classmates got expelled?" "Yes, and everyone's glad."

ctx.s: 多年逍遥法外的贪官最终落网，市民纷纷说这件事{大快人心}。
ctx.en: The corrupt official who had evaded justice for years was finally caught, and residents said it was a great relief to them all.

ctx.s: 警方这次打掉了一个电信诈骗团伙，{大快人心}，也给其他骗子敲响了警钟。
ctx.en: The police broke up a phone-scam ring, to everyone's satisfaction, and it is a warning to other fraudsters.

bad.s: 今天天气很好，我们去公园玩，{大快人心}。
bad.en: (meant: the weather was nice and we had fun in the park)
bad.why: It is the public's satisfaction at a wrongdoer being punished, not ordinary personal fun or happiness.

bad.s: 他考上了理想的大学，全家人都觉得{大快人心}。
bad.en: (meant: the family was overjoyed at his exam result)
bad.why: Good news about a success is not what it describes; it needs a bad person getting what they deserve.

lit: to go deep into people's hearts

use.how: Used as a predicate about an idea, value, image or slogan that the public has accepted deeply: 环保理念已经深入人心。

near.diff: 家喻户晓 means everyone knows of it; 深入人心 means people have taken it to heart and believe in it.

cue: Twenty years ago few people sorted their rubbish; now almost everyone believes it matters and does it without being told.

ctx.s: 垃圾分类的观念已经{深入人心}。
ctx.en: The idea of sorting rubbish has taken firm hold among people.

ctx.s: 这部电视剧里的老师形象{深入人心}，很多人因此当了老师。
ctx.en: The teacher in this TV series won people's hearts, and many became teachers because of her.

ctx.s: “安全第一”这句口号人人都会说，可它真的{深入人心}了吗？
ctx.en: Everyone can recite the slogan "safety first", but has it really taken root in people's hearts?

ctx.s: 经过多年宣传，男女平等的思想逐渐{深入人心}。
ctx.en: After years of promotion, the idea of equality between men and women gradually took root in people's minds.

ctx.s: 这个品牌之所以成功，是因为它“质量可靠”的形象早已{深入人心}。
ctx.en: The brand succeeded because its image of reliable quality has long been firmly established in consumers' minds.

ctx.s: 老校长说：“好的规矩，要靠大家认同，才能真正{深入人心}。”
ctx.en: The old principal said, "Good rules only truly take root when everyone believes in them."

bad.s: 他昨天受的伤很重，刀口{深入人心}。
bad.en: (meant: the knife wound was very deep)
bad.why: It is about ideas taking hold in people's minds, never about a physical wound or depth.

bad.s: 这个新闻刚发布五分钟，就已经{深入人心}了。
bad.en: (meant: the news spread everywhere within minutes)
bad.why: It describes deep, lasting acceptance built over time, not news spreading quickly within minutes.

mean: approachable and easy to talk to
lit: plain and easy, close to people

story.text: When the Duke of Zhou's son Boqin was enfeoffed in Lu, he took three years to report on his rule, because he had changed the local customs and rites. Jiang Taigong, enfeoffed in Qi, reported in five months, saying he had simplified the rites and followed local ways. The Duke of Zhou sighed that Lu would one day serve Qi: if government is not simple and easy, the people will not come close; if it is plain, easy and close to the people, they will surely turn to it. In the original the phrase reads "close to the people" rather than "close to others".

use.how: Used as a predicate or attribute praising someone of higher status who is friendly and unpretentious with ordinary people: 校长很平易近人。

near.diff: 和蔼可亲 stresses a kind, gentle manner; 平易近人 stresses that a person of rank does not put on airs.

cue: The company's famous founder eats in the staff canteen, chats with interns and never mentions his title.

ctx.s: 我们的新经理虽然职位高，却很{平易近人}，大家都喜欢找他聊天。
ctx.en: Our new manager is very approachable; everyone likes to go and chat with him.

ctx.s: 没想到这位大明星这么{平易近人}，还主动跟粉丝合影。
ctx.en: I never expected the big star to be so down-to-earth; she even offered to take photos with fans.

ctx.s: 那位老教授学问很大，却一点架子也没有，非常{平易近人}。
ctx.en: The old professor is very learned but has no airs at all; he is very easy to talk to.

ctx.s: “院长会不会很严肃？”“放心吧，他是个{平易近人}的人。”
ctx.en: "Is the dean very stern?" "Don't worry, he's very approachable."

ctx.s: 市长常常走进普通居民家里，这种{平易近人}的作风赢得了大家的信任。
ctx.en: The mayor often visits ordinary residents' homes, and this unpretentious style has won people's trust.

ctx.s: 一位好的领导，既要有能力，也要{平易近人}，让下属敢说真话。
ctx.en: A good leader should be capable and also approachable, so that staff dare to speak honestly.

bad.s: 这道数学题很{平易近人}，大家都会做。
bad.en: (meant: this maths problem is easy)
bad.why: It describes a person's manner toward others, not how easy a task or problem is.

bad.s: 我家小狗很{平易近人}，见谁都摇尾巴。
bad.en: (meant: my puppy is friendly to everyone)
bad.why: It praises a person, usually someone of higher status, for not putting on airs; it is not used for animals.

mean: to bully others by trading on a powerful backer
lit: the fox borrows the tiger's might

story.text: A tiger caught a fox. The fox said: Heaven has made me king of the beasts, so if you eat me you defy Heaven; walk behind me and see whether the animals dare to stay. The tiger followed, and every animal fled at the sight of them. The tiger thought they feared the fox, not knowing they feared the tiger. Jiang Yi told this fable to King Xuan of Chu: the north feared the king's army, not his minister Zhao Xixu.

use.how: Used as a predicate or attribute criticising someone who bosses others around on the strength of a superior or powerful relative: 他不过是狐假虎威。

near.diff: 仗势欺人 is bullying by relying on any power, including one's own; 狐假虎威 stresses that the power belongs to someone else.

cue: The boss's nephew joined last month as a junior clerk, yet he orders everyone around and says, "My uncle will hear about this."

ctx.s: 他仗着舅舅是校长，在班里{狐假虎威}，其实自己什么本事也没有。
ctx.en: Because his uncle is the headmaster, he throws his weight around in class, though he himself has no ability at all.

ctx.s: 别怕她，她只是{狐假虎威}，自己根本做不了主。
ctx.en: Don't be afraid of her; she's just borrowing someone else's authority and can't decide anything herself.

ctx.s: 老板一出差，那个秘书就没法再{狐假虎威}了。
ctx.en: As soon as the boss went away on business, the secretary could no longer use his name to push people around.

ctx.s: “你算什么？不过是借着经理的名头{狐假虎威}罢了！”
ctx.en: "Who do you think you are? You're just using the manager's name to bully us!"

ctx.s: 小说里的管家{狐假虎威}，对下人百般刁难，见了主人却低声下气。
ctx.en: In the novel the steward uses his master's power to torment the servants, yet grovels before the master himself.

ctx.s: 有些人自己没什么权力，却靠着和领导的关系{狐假虎威}，这种风气必须改。
ctx.en: Some people with no power of their own trade on their ties with the leadership to intimidate others; this practice has to change.

bad.s: 他自己当上了总经理，开始{狐假虎威}，对员工大喊大叫。
bad.en: (meant: once he became general manager himself he began bullying staff)
bad.why: The power here is his own; the idiom needs someone borrowing a more powerful backer's authority.

bad.s: 老虎在山上{狐假虎威}，动物们都很害怕。
bad.en: (meant: the tiger on the mountain was fearsome)
bad.why: It is a figurative criticism of a person, not a description of a real tiger being frightening.

lit: refined and gentle, full of courtesy

use.how: Used as a predicate, attribute or adverbial (彬彬有礼地) about someone's polite, cultivated manners: 他对人彬彬有礼。

near.diff: 落落大方 is being relaxed and natural, not shy; 彬彬有礼 is being polite and well-mannered.

cue: The young man holds the door, greets each guest by name, thanks the waiter and never interrupts anyone.

ctx.s: 这个孩子见了长辈总是{彬彬有礼}。
ctx.en: This child is always polite and well-mannered with his elders.

ctx.s: 酒店的服务员{彬彬有礼}地把我们带到了房间。
ctx.en: The hotel attendant courteously showed us to our room.

ctx.s: 他看起来{彬彬有礼}，说话也很客气，大家对他印象都不错。
ctx.en: He seems courteous and speaks politely, so everyone has a good impression of him.

ctx.s: “你男朋友人怎么样？”“很{彬彬有礼}，见了我爸妈又是问好又是倒茶。”
ctx.en: "What's your boyfriend like?" "Very courteous; when he met my parents he greeted them properly and poured them tea."

ctx.s: 谈判时，对方代表始终{彬彬有礼}，但在关键问题上寸步不让。
ctx.en: During the negotiations the other side's representative was unfailingly polite but would not give an inch on the key issues.

ctx.s: 一个{彬彬有礼}的人，不一定就是真心待你的人。
ctx.en: Someone who is courteous is not necessarily someone who sincerely cares about you.

bad.s: 这家餐厅的菜{彬彬有礼}，味道很好。
bad.en: (meant: the restaurant's dishes are refined and tasty)
bad.why: It describes a person's manners, not food or things.

bad.s: 他把房间收拾得{彬彬有礼}，干干净净。
bad.en: (meant: he tidied his room neatly)
bad.why: It describes a person's courteous manners toward others, not how neat or orderly a place is.

mean: natural and poised, at ease with others
lit: open and easy, generous in bearing

use.how: Used as a predicate, attribute or adverbial about someone's natural, unselfconscious manner in public or with strangers: 她回答问题落落大方。

near.diff: 彬彬有礼 is being polite and well-mannered; 落落大方 is being relaxed and natural rather than shy or awkward.

cue: A sixteen-year-old student is interviewed on live television and answers calmly and naturally, with no blushing or stammering.

ctx.s: 她第一次上台演讲，却一点也不紧张，{落落大方}。
ctx.en: It was her first time giving a speech on stage, yet she wasn't nervous at all; she was poised and natural.

ctx.s: 面试时要{落落大方}，不要低着头说话。
ctx.en: In an interview you should be natural and at ease; don't talk with your head down.

ctx.s: 这个小女孩见了客人不躲不藏，{落落大方}地打招呼。
ctx.en: The little girl didn't hide from the guests but greeted them naturally and confidently.

ctx.s: “新来的同事怎么样？”“人很开朗，说话{落落大方}的。”
ctx.en: "What's the new colleague like?" "Very outgoing, and she speaks with real ease."

ctx.s: 记者问到尴尬的问题，他{落落大方}地承认了自己的错误。
ctx.en: When the reporter asked an awkward question, he admitted his mistake openly and without embarrassment.

ctx.s: 她穿着简单，举止{落落大方}，给评委留下了很深的印象。
ctx.en: She was simply dressed and carried herself with natural poise, which made a strong impression on the judges.

bad.s: 他请客很{落落大方}，一顿饭花了好几千。
bad.en: (meant: he was generous with money when treating people)
bad.why: The second half alone can mean generous with money, but the idiom only describes a relaxed, natural manner, not spending freely.

bad.s: 这件衣服太{落落大方}了，我穿着又宽又长。
bad.en: (meant: this garment is too big and loose for me)
bad.why: It praises a natural, easy bearing; it does not mean large or loose-fitting.

lit: a knife hidden inside a smile

story.text: Li Yifu, a chief minister under Emperor Gaozong of Tang, looked mild and respectful and always smiled when he spoke with people, but he was narrow-minded and vicious, and secretly ruined anyone who crossed him. People of the time said there was a knife in his smile, and because he was soft on the outside and harmful within, they also called him Li the Cat.

use.how: Used as a predicate or attribute criticising someone who is friendly to your face while plotting to harm you: 这个人笑里藏刀。

near.diff: 口蜜腹剑 stresses sweet words with evil intent; 笑里藏刀 stresses a friendly smiling manner hiding it. They are very close.

cue: Your colleague always greets you with a big smile, and you later learn she has been quietly telling the boss you are unreliable.

ctx.s: 别看他整天对你笑眯眯的，他其实是{笑里藏刀}。
ctx.en: Don't be fooled by how he beams at you all day; he's hiding a knife behind that smile.

ctx.s: 我最怕{笑里藏刀}的人，当面一套，背后一套。
ctx.en: What I fear most are people who smile while plotting against you: one thing to your face, another behind your back.

ctx.s: 电视剧里的那个皇后{笑里藏刀}，看得观众直起鸡皮疙瘩。
ctx.en: The empress in that TV drama smiles sweetly while scheming, and she gives the audience goosebumps.

ctx.s: “他今天突然请我吃饭，会不会{笑里藏刀}啊？”
ctx.en: "He suddenly invited me to dinner today. Could there be a knife behind that smile?"

ctx.s: 直到被对手抢走了客户，他才明白对方当初{笑里藏刀}。
ctx.en: Only when his rival stole his clients did he realise the man's friendliness had hidden malice all along.

ctx.s: 那些满脸堆笑却{笑里藏刀}的朋友，比说话难听但真诚的人可怕得多。
ctx.en: Friends who greet you all smiles while scheming against you are far more dangerous than people who speak bluntly but sincerely.

bad.s: 厨师{笑里藏刀}，一边笑一边切菜。
bad.en: (meant: the chef smiled while chopping vegetables)
bad.why: The knife is figurative; it means hidden malice behind friendliness, not literally holding a knife.

bad.s: 他心里很难过，但还是{笑里藏刀}，不让别人担心。
bad.en: (meant: he hid his sadness behind a smile)
bad.why: It is hidden hostility toward others, not putting on a brave smile to hide one's own sadness.

mean: to probe or hint by indirect questions
lit: to knock at the side and strike from the flank

use.how: Used as a predicate or adverbial (旁敲侧击地问) about getting information or making a point indirectly instead of asking or saying it straight out.

near.diff: 拐弯抹角 criticises talking round in circles; 旁敲侧击 is a deliberate tactic of indirect questions or hints to find out or suggest something.

cue: You want to know if your friend has a girlfriend, so instead of asking, you ask who he went to the cinema with and why he has been so cheerful lately.

ctx.s: 妈妈{旁敲侧击}地问我最近是不是谈恋爱了。
ctx.en: Mum dropped hints, asking in a roundabout way whether I'd started seeing someone.

ctx.s: 我想知道他的工资，又不好直接问，只能{旁敲侧击}。
ctx.en: I wanted to know his salary but couldn't ask outright, so I could only probe indirectly.

ctx.s: 老板{旁敲侧击}了好几次，意思是希望我们周末加班。
ctx.en: The boss hinted several times that he wanted us to work over the weekend.

ctx.s: “你别{旁敲侧击}了，想知道我考了多少分就直接问吧。”
ctx.en: "Stop fishing with roundabout questions. If you want to know my score, just ask."

ctx.s: 警察没有直接提案子，而是{旁敲侧击}，从他的回答里找破绽。
ctx.en: The police didn't mention the case directly but probed indirectly, looking for holes in his answers.

ctx.s: 同事们{旁敲侧击}地打听新经理的来历，可谁也没问出什么。
ctx.en: Colleagues made roundabout inquiries about the new manager's background, but nobody found out anything.

bad.s: 他在门外{旁敲侧击}，敲了半天门也没人开。
bad.en: (meant: he knocked on the door for ages)
bad.why: It is figurative, about indirect questions or hints, not physically knocking on something.

bad.s: 他{旁敲侧击}地对我说：“你明天必须交报告。”
bad.en: (meant: he told me directly that the report was due)
bad.why: A blunt, direct order is the opposite of what it means; it describes hints and indirect probing.

mean: to cut corners on labour and materials
lit: to steal on work and reduce materials

use.how: Used as a predicate or attribute criticising builders, makers or workers who skimp on work or materials to save money; also figuratively of any job done with corners cut.

near.diff: 敷衍了事 is doing a task perfunctorily to get it over with; 偷工减料 is deliberately skimping on labour or materials, often for profit.

cue: A new school building cracks within a year, and inspectors find the builder used less steel and cheaper cement than the contract required.

ctx.s: 这座桥才建好两年就出现裂缝，肯定是{偷工减料}了。
ctx.en: The bridge has cracks only two years after it was built; they must have skimped on work and materials.

ctx.s: 装修的时候你得经常去看看，防止工人{偷工减料}。
ctx.en: During the renovation you need to check in often, so the workers don't cut corners.

ctx.s: 这家店的包子越来越小，馅也少了，明显在{偷工减料}。
ctx.en: This shop's buns keep getting smaller with less filling; they're clearly skimping.

ctx.s: “这么便宜的价格，他们会不会{偷工减料}？”
ctx.en: "At such a low price, won't they cut corners?"

ctx.s: 调查发现，开发商为了多赚钱，在楼房的地基上{偷工减料}。
ctx.en: The investigation found that the developer had skimped on the building's foundations to make more money.

ctx.s: 写论文也不能{偷工减料}，该查的资料一份都不能少。
ctx.en: You can't cut corners on a thesis either; you have to consult every source you should.

bad.s: 为了节约用电，我们决定{偷工减料}，晚上早点关灯。
bad.en: (meant: to save electricity we turn the lights off early)
bad.why: It is a criticism of skimping on a job's quality, not a neutral word for saving resources.

bad.s: 他工作效率很高，每天都{偷工减料}，提前完成任务。
bad.en: (meant: he is efficient and finishes early)
bad.why: It is never praise for efficiency; it means lowering quality by cheating on work or materials.

mean: sloppy and long-winded, not clean or quick

use.how: Used as a predicate or adverbial, often after 不 or 别, about writing, speech or actions that are drawn-out and indecisive: 做事不要拖泥带水。

near.diff: 干净利落 is its opposite: neat, quick and decisive.

cue: Your colleague's emails ramble for pages before reaching the point, and every decision she makes comes with three rounds of second thoughts.

ctx.s: 他做事从不{拖泥带水}，说干就干。
ctx.en: He never dithers; once he decides to do something, he does it.

ctx.s: 这篇文章写得{拖泥带水}，读了半天也不知道重点在哪儿。
ctx.en: This article is long-winded and muddled; I read it for ages and still couldn't find the point.

ctx.s: 既然已经决定分手，就别再{拖泥带水}了。
ctx.en: Since you've decided to break up, don't drag it out any longer.

ctx.s: “你说话能不能别这么{拖泥带水}？直接告诉我结果。”
ctx.en: "Can you stop rambling? Just tell me the result."

ctx.s: 这场比赛主队的进攻{拖泥带水}，错过了好几次机会。
ctx.en: The home side's attacks were slow and messy, and they wasted several chances.

ctx.s: 新领导处理问题干脆利落，和以前{拖泥带水}的作风完全不同。
ctx.en: The new leader deals with problems crisply, quite unlike the old dithering way of doing things.

bad.s: 下雨天路不好走，我的鞋子{拖泥带水}。
bad.en: (meant: my shoes were muddy and wet)
bad.why: It is figurative, about sloppy, drawn-out work or speech, not actual mud and water on shoes.

bad.s: 他做菜非常{拖泥带水}，又快又好吃。
bad.en: (meant: he cooks quickly and well)
bad.why: It is a criticism of slow, messy work, so it cannot praise speed or skill.
